transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (CTO, Novus Retail), Priya Shah (ML Eng), Marisol Gomez (Infra Lead), Luke Tan (Product)

Summary:
Quick demo focused on edge cases: extremely long context (50k-100k tokens), sustained high TPS (500-2k TPS bursts), streaming/backpressure behavior and timeouts. Discussed dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, fallback strategies, and next steps for a pilot benchmark.

Topics: long context handling, KV cache, quantization effects, batching and throughput, streaming backpressure and client timeouts, failure modes and graceful degradation, security/VPC and SSO.

Action items (recap): see metadata above.

Transcript:
00:00 Samir: okay hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm Samir from Redwood, i'll kick us off, Laura and Diego are here to go deep on the runtime and streaming stuff, and Alex and team we appreciate the time
00:12 Alex: yeah thanks Samir, we've been excited to see the edge cases deck, priya's going to want to dig into the long context perf, marisol will hit infra constraints, and luke is here for product fit
00:25 Laura: cool, quick agenda — show the console shortcuts for model variants, then run two short demos: a 60k token context job and a high TPS streaming scenario that simulates our webhook fanout, and then go into mitigation patterns for backpressure/timeouts
00:40 Priya: can you clarify, when you say 60k tokens — is that a single prompt window, or are you stitching multiple docs? our use case stitches customer history plus multi-turn conversation so effective context is ~80k sometimes
00:55 Laura: both actually, we see both single huge contexts and stitched session contexts. our runtime uses KV caching and prefix caching to reduce recompute, but that still has memory/kv tradeoffs. we're going to demo both patterns.
01:10 Diego: note i might mangle acronyms — KV cache sometimes shows up as K-V-ish cache in logs — sorry for the automatic transcript quirks
01:24 Marisol: infra note — we have strict egress caps on our prod VPC and peaky bursts can hit our NAT throughput causing tail latency, that's the real risk for us
01:38 Samir: totally understood. we'll show the Router policies and dedicated capacity options. for high burst TPS we recommend Dedicated with auto-burst + burst queueing; hosted can do it but you'll see variable latency and you'll need to tune client timeouts
01:55 Alex: about timeouts — our stack has 90s request timeouts on the client side; we can't push to 5 minutes easily. how do you handle streaming partial responses vs full completion?
02:10 Laura: good question. we support chunked streaming so clients get partial tokens early. if a backend request exceeds client timeout we'll send a streaming partial + a resumable pointer — in practice we also expose canary fallbacks to smaller models to ensure something returns within the timeout window
02:30 Priya: resumable pointer? can you explain, does that mean state is checkpointed server side so we can reattach?
02:36 Laura: yes, we persist short KV checkpoints for long-context jobs. it's not a full snapshot for every token but we can resume generation from a saved prefix state; that helps with long-running completions and reconnects. there are tradeoffs around retention and cost
02:52 Priya: got it. what's the memory footprint for 60k-80k contexts on your preferred quantized model? we plan to run 8B-13B variants in prod
03:05 Diego: rough numbers — on Ampere A100-ish hardware with 8-bit quant the working set for a 13B model with 80k effective tokens hits ~60-90GB of model+kv memory depending on kv shard and whether we use transient offload. on L4/RTX it varies. this is why we recommend kernel selection and tailored quant profiles per workload
03:30 Marisol: so is that A100 dedicated only? our environment is GCP with limited A100 reservations, mostly T4/NVIDIA L4 equivalent in region X
03:42 Laura: we can route by region and hardware class; for peak burst we often route to compatible variant that can serve the job with slightly higher latency but within your budget. also Redwood Dedicated lets you pick a pool with preferred hardware. we'll include a mapping table in the follow-up docs
03:58 Luke: curious about observed tail latencies under peak. if we pump 2k TPS for 2 minutes, what's the 95/99?
04:08 Diego: depends a lot on batching and prefix reuse. if you have high prefix commonality (shared lead tokens, same prompt template) the batching engine does wonders and 95th stays low. if every request is unique you'll see a wider spread. we have internal benchmarks — for synthetic workloads with 1-2k TPS and 2-3 token output lengths we keep 95th ~200-300ms on Dedicated; for large context completions the 95th jumps to seconds, which is expected
04:35 Priya: okay, can you demo the streaming backpressure behavior? like when our consumer can't keep up and the socket slow drains — how does Redwood handle TCP buffer backpressure vs internal queueing
04:47 Laura: yes — let me share the console. (screen share) here's the streaming endpoint, i have a simulated slow consumer and a spike generator. i'll keep a timestamped log on the right.
05:02 Laura: starting high TPS spike now — notice we throttle at the edge and apply backpressure signals to internal batcher. when client ack rate drops below a threshold we start buffering up to a configured limit, then switch to adaptive chunking and reduce per-client tokens per chunk.
05:22 Alex: what's your buffer limit before you start dropping or failing? our SLA won't allow silent drops
05:28 Diego: default is conservative — we buffer up to a per-connection window (configurable) and then apply circuit-breaker policies. if the queue is full we can return a 429 with a retry-after or return a partial stream + resumable pointer. silent drops are not the default
05:45 Marisol: network costs matter — buffering a lot increases egress and memory. we need a clear billing model for retransmits/resumables
05:54 Samir: noted. billing model for resumable payloads and replays is something we include in SOW pilot pricing. we'll be explicit about egress and storage cost assumptions.
06:10 Priya: can you show how fallback to smaller models is configured automatically? we worry about quality regression but prefer something over nothing in timeouts
06:20 Laura: demo time. (switches) here's a routing policy: primary model = redwood-13b-q4, fallback chain = redwood-7b-q4 -> redwood-3b-q2. you can set accuracy thresholds, and also a hard timeout threshold to trigger fallback. i'm going to trigger a synthetic latency on the 13b and show the switch.
06:45 Laura: triggering now — notice stream stalls, then within configured threshold the router launches parallel request to 7b and we return the 7b stream while 13b completes background. the client sees a continuous stream from whichever returns first (we annotate token source metadata)
07:06 Luke: that seems useful. how often do you recommend running quality evals when you have rolling model updates and quant changes?
07:14 Samir: recommend nightly quick checks on core prompts and a full regression suite weekly for prod-critical prompts; Redwood Optimize can automate alerting for quality regressions and tie to rollouts
07:27 Alex: security — if we use Dedicated in our VPC, how is KMS handled and do you store any customer plaintext?
07:36 Laura: Dedicated with Private mode offers control plane in your VPC and optional on-prem agent; no model inputs are stored by default unless you opt-in for logs; keys can be customer-managed in KMS/HSM and audit logs are available. we'll share SOC2 pack and HSM integration docs in the follow-up
07:56 Priya: another perf question — how do you avoid OOMs when kv state grows during multi-turn sessions? we have sessions that accumulate thousands of tokens across hours
08:10 Diego: strategies: prefix trimming and eviction policies, checkpointing to disk + fast restart, and selective kv compaction based on token salience. also quantized kv encoding helps. it's a balance: aggressive eviction reduces context fidelity; we can tune per-app.
08:30 Marisol: will that add latency if we checkpoint to disk? our disks are network attached in our infra and add variability
08:38 Laura: yes slightly; we use asynchronous checkpointing and warm caches on resume to reduce tail. for ultra-low tail you want dedicated NVMe local or memory-mapped offload solutions — we'll outline options in the recommendation doc
08:55 Priya: curious about telemetry — can we get token-level latency breakdowns so we can see where the time is spent?
09:03 Diego: yes, Console tracing includes token-level timing, per-batcher metrics, and RK (router key) traces that map requests across shards. you can export traces to your APM too; note the tracer labels sometimes get fuzzy in the auto transcript so forgive the naming
09:22 Alex: what about SDK behavior on transient 504/timeouts? our current retries are naive and cause duplicates downstream
09:30 Laura: Redwood SDK supports idempotency keys and resumable stream reconnection logic. for HTTP clients we advise a short exponential backoff with jitter and prefer resumable semantics over blind retries. for webhooks we recommend dedupe at the receiver side as well
09:47 Luke: can you show an example client config that avoids retry storms but still gets completions in face of backpressure?
09:54 Diego: yes, here's a recommended config — base timeout 30s, streaming keepalive 15s, backoff 500ms->2s max, idempotency key per user-session. also set acceptable partial-return behavior in product design
10:15 Priya: performance numbers for quantization — do you have comparisons for q4 vs q8 on 13B with 60k context?
10:23 Diego: short answer: q4 gives 1.6-1.9x memory reduction with small perf hit, q8 is higher memory but slightly faster on some kernels. on very long contexts q4 tends to be best overall for throughput but we recommend per-workload microbenchmarks
10:40 Samir: let's do a quick live 60k context generation — i'll paste a stitched session, we'll watch memory and stream behavior; Priya please watch for token fidelity and Marisol watch infra metrics
10:55 (demo)
11:00 Laura: starting generation, note timestamp 11:00:00 in logs
11:12 Priya: i'm seeing a larger than expected token drop on one of the stitched segments, maybe alignment issue, audio note: the transcript picked up 'align mint' earlier
11:30 Diego: that's likely tokenizer boundary differences across model variants, also combined stitching order matters; we'll surface tokenizer-normalization guidance in the follow up
11:45 Marisol: infra alert — NAT throughput spiked and we saw 504s from our edge for a few seconds
11:52 Alex: how do you differentiate between network 504 and runtime timeouts in your logs? we need clear root cause for SREs
12:00 Laura: our traces annotate origin — network-level 504s flagged at the edge, runtime timeouts flagged in the service trace. we also correlate with per-token timing to show where latency occurs. we'll give an example trace in the docs
12:18 Priya: can you quantify how resumable pointer replay affects customer-visible latency? i.e., if we cut and reconnect do users see a delay or double tokens
12:27 Diego: typically resumable reconnect adds a small delta (100-500ms) because we resume from a saved prefix and replay the last N tokens for safety. duplicates are guarded by idempotency keys but clients need to handle possible overlap; we'll include example client logic
12:45 Luke: what about rate limiting and fair share across customers in a shared pool? we have multi-tenant spikes normally and want to avoid noisy neighbor issues
12:54 Laura: router supports per-customer rate limits and weighted fair-queuing; Dedicated pools can be isolated at tenant level. for shared hosted pools we recommend per-route token caps and burst credit system
13:12 Alex: ok looks promising. what's the pilot timeline if we proceed?
13:18 Samir: typical pilot — 2-4 weeks to scope and get data, then a 2-week benchmark with Redwood Dedicated in your region, followed by a 30-day pilot SLA. we can compress if you have infra ready and provide sample payloads quickly
13:34 Priya: we'll need the benchmark template and sample harness to run against our VPC in region X
13:40 Samir: action: Samir to send benchmark template, Laura to provide canary config + quant profiles, Diego to prepare mapping of hardware compatibilities. Marisol to confirm network constraints.
13:55 Marisol: one last question — do you support sidecar/on-prem package for air-gapped workloads?
14:02 Laura: yes we have a private on-prem package; it's slightly different in terms of features (some tracing shipped over collectors) but supports the same routing and caching primitives. we'll include a whitepaper.
14:18 Alex: thanks everyone, that was thorough. we'll review and come back with availability for the benchmark next week.
14:26 Samir: thanks — we'll follow up with the security pack, SOW draft and benchmark harness. thanks all.

End of call.
